questions.stem: Reflection happens when a wave arrives at a boundary and:

options.text: passes into the new medium and bends
options.explanation: That describes refraction.

options.text: stays in the original medium, bouncing back
options.explanation: Reflected waves do not cross into the second medium.
The wave continues, redirected.
Dispersion is a separate effect.

questions.stem: The law of reflection states that:

options.text: angle of incidence = angle of refraction
options.explanation: That confuses reflection with refraction.

options.text: angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection
options.explanation: No doubling exists in the law.

options.text: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
options.explanation: That equality is the law, both angles from the normal.

options.text: the angles add to ninety degrees
options.explanation: No fixed sum is part of the law.

questions.stem: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured between the ray and:

options.explanation: Measuring from the surface is the classic error.
The incident ray cannot measure its own angle.
Wavefronts are drawing aids, not angle references.
The normal is the reference line for all such angles.

questions.stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 35 degrees from the normal. It leaves at:

options.text: 35 degrees from the normal on the other side
options.explanation: The reflection angle equals the incidence angle.
That subtracts from ninety unnecessarily.
No doubling applies.

options.text: 35 degrees measured from the mirror surface
options.explanation: Angles are quoted from the normal, not the surface.
Sound and water waves reflect too.
Longitudinal waves reflect as echoes.
Reflection is universal across the wave families.

options.text: none, it is a light-only effect
options.explanation: The spec statement is explicitly about all waves.

questions.stem: State the law of reflection in words.
questions.modelAnswer: The incidence angle equals the reflection angle, both measured from the normal.
The normal is the construction line at right angles (ninety degrees) to the boundary from which angles are measured.

questions.stem: Explain why measuring reflection angles from the mirror surface instead of the normal gives the wrong comparison.
questions.modelAnswer: The law compares angles defined from the normal, so measuring from the surface gives each angle as its complement to ninety degrees; two unequal incidence and reflection angles could then appear equal, hiding the true geometry.

questions.stem: A tree stands by a calm lake and its image appears below it in the water. Name the effect and state the equality that governs each ray involved.
questions.modelAnswer: The image is produced by reflection at the water surface; every ray obeys the law of reflection, leaving at an angle from the normal equal to the angle at which it arrived.

questions.stem: On a ray diagram, the arrow of the incident ray points:

options.explanation: That is the reflected ray convention.
Incident rays travel into the boundary.
No convention points rays along the surface here.
Each ray carries one direction arrow.

questions.stem: Light passes from air into glass. The refracted ray bends:

options.explanation: That is the glass-to-air direction.
No bending happens only along the normal.
That would be reflection, not refraction.
Into the denser medium the ray bends towards the normal.

questions.stem: Light leaves the glass block back into air. The emerging ray bends:

options.explanation: Into the less dense medium the ray bends away from the normal.
That is the air-to-glass direction.
That special case is not the general exit behaviour.
Rays bend linearly at flat boundaries.

options.text: frequency and speed, but not wavelength
options.explanation: Frequency is the survivor; wavelength follows speed.
Frequency never changes on refraction.

options.text: speed and wavelength, but not frequency
options.explanation: The medium changes the speed and the wavelength rescales with it.
A speed change is the cause of the bending.

questions.stem: A ray hits a boundary exactly along the normal. It:

options.explanation: It is already on the normal; there is nothing to bend towards.
Partial reflection may occur, but the listed behaviour is straight-through transmission.
The wave continues into the new medium.
Along the normal there is no direction change on refraction.

questions.stem: State the bending rule for light entering a denser medium.
State what happens to the frequency of light during refraction.
Explain why a pencil standing in a glass of water looks bent at the surface.
questions.modelAnswer: Light from the underwater part leaves the water and bends away from the normal into the air, so the rays reaching your eye come from a shifted apparent direction and the pencil appears bent at the boundary.

questions.stem: A ray diagram must show a beam travelling air-to-glass-to-air through a rectangular block. Sketch description: state the bend at each boundary and the arrow directions.
questions.modelAnswer: At the air-to-glass face the ray bends towards the normal as it enters; at the glass-to-air face it bends away from the normal as it leaves; the incident arrow points at the first boundary and the emerging arrow points away from the block on the far side.
